{{Short description|Mathematical property}}
{{Refimprove|date=March 2015}}
In [[topology]], a branch of mathematics, a [[topological space]] ''X'' is said to be '''simply connected at infinity''' if for any [[compact space|compact]] subset ''C'' of ''X'', there is a compact set ''D'' in ''X'' containing ''C'' so that the induced map on [[fundamental group]]s

: <math> \pi_1(X-D) \to \pi_1(X-C)</math>

is the zero map.  Intuitively, this is the property that loops far away from a small subspace of ''X'' can be collapsed, no matter how bad the small subspace is.

The [[Whitehead manifold]] is an example of a 3-[[manifold]] that is [[contractible]] but not simply connected at infinity. Since this property is invariant under [[homeomorphism]], this proves that the Whitehead manifold is not homeomorphic to '''R'''<sup>3</sup>. 

However, it is a theorem of [[John R. Stallings]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.math.rutgers.edu/~sferry/ps/geotop.pdf |title=Theory : Chapter 10 |publisher=Math.rutgers.edu |accessdate=2015-03-08}}</ref> that for <math>n \geq 5</math>, a contractible ''n''-manifold is homeomorphic to '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> precisely when it is simply connected at infinity.
